text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Here's something most of us never think about. You turn on a tap in a new suburb outside a big Texas city, and clean water comes out. You flush, and it goes away. Somebody, somewhere, checked that the chlorine level was right this morning. Somebody walked past a lift station and listened to the pumps. Somebody filed a report with the state saying it was all done properly.

speaker: JAMES
text: And in a surprising number of places, that somebody doesn't work for the town. They work for a private company that the town or the local utility district has hired to run the whole system on its behalf. Operators, maintenance crews, lab sampling, compliance paperwork, sometimes even the water bills.

speaker: NORA
text: That's the world of today's company. Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Today it's USA Water, a contract operator of water and wastewater systems based in the Houston area, working mainly across Texas and the Southeast of the United States.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: company and private equity announcements, trade press, industry research pages and a couple of data aggregators. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. When a figure comes from an aggregator or a vendor, we'll flag it. And nothing here is investment advice.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'll add an honest warning up front. USA Water is a private company that says very little in public. So today is partly an episode about what we know, and partly about what we don't, and we'll be clear about which is which.

speaker: NORA
text: Good. So give me the one-sentence version.

speaker: JAMES
text: USA Water runs water and wastewater systems for municipalities and utility districts under contract. They own the pipes and the plants. USA Water supplies the licensed people, the maintenance, the compliance work and, in some cases, the billing, so that the water keeps flowing and the regulators stay satisfied.

speaker: NORA
text: And why is it interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three reasons. The water industry has a real workforce problem, with fewer licensed operators coming through. The market is consolidating, and USA Water is a buy-and-build platform. And AI is starting to be talked about as a tool for what the trade press calls the augmented operator. That's the question we want to explore: what does AI look like for a company whose product is, fundamentally, skilled people on site?

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the basics. Where is it, how big is it, who runs it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Even the basics come with a caveat. The headquarters is listed in two places. The firm that founded it, the 2020 launch announcement and one aggregator say Houston. Levine Leichtman's own pages and some trade press say Rosenberg, Texas, which is southwest of Houston and is where the Si Environmental office sits. So the fair way to say it is the Houston metro area.

speaker: NORA
text: Si Environmental. We'll come back to that name, I assume.

speaker: JAMES
text: We will, it's the heart of the business. On size, there's no public revenue figure. One aggregator, Crunchbase, estimates between one hundred and one and two hundred and fifty employees, and I'd treat that as a rough estimate only. We didn't find a public customer count for USA Water as a whole either. What we do have is that Si Environmental served more than eighty utility districts at the time it was acquired in 2020, according to the announcement then.

speaker: NORA
text: And leadership?

speaker: JAMES
text: The chief executive is Jeff Haley, who stayed on when Levine Leichtman bought the business in 2024. The leadership page for Si Environmental also names Juan Alexander as president, Chris Wilson as chief operating officer, Jeff Schultz as chief financial officer, Nathan White as vice president of strategy and development, and Ross Madia as vice president of billing and technical services.

speaker: NORA
text: That last title is interesting for our purposes.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. It's the closest thing to a technology leadership role we could see in public. And it tells you billing is treated as a real service line, not an afterthought. One more note: one aggregator still lists Sohail Alyasin as founder and chief executive. He did lead the company when it was formed in 2020, but that listing looks out of date.

speaker: NORA
text: You said the company's site wasn't something you could review.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. We weren't able to check the USA Water holding company website directly, so anything it says about itself, we haven't verified. Most of what we know comes from the 2020 and 2024 deal announcements, the Si Environmental team page, and industry sources.

speaker: NORA
text: So what does the business look like on the ground?

speaker: JAMES
text: Picture a lot of relatively small systems. A water plant here, a wastewater treatment plant there, wells, storage tanks, lift stations that pump sewage uphill, miles of pipe. Each one belongs to a public body. USA Water's crews run them, maintain them, take samples, fix things when they break, and handle the regulatory reporting. Levine Leichtman described the services as non-discretionary, and that's the key word. You don't get to skip water treatment in a bad year.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the history. You said 2020.

speaker: JAMES
text: The story starts earlier, with Si Environmental, which was founded in 2012. It built up a contract operations business serving utility districts in the Houston area. Then in October 2020, a private equity firm called Warren Equity Partners formed USA Water together with a group of industry executives, and in the same month acquired Si Environmental as the founding business.

speaker: NORA
text: So USA Water was created as a platform from day one.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. That's a classic private equity move. You form a holding company with an operating team, you buy a strong anchor business, and then you add more operators over time. The name USA Water is quite deliberately bigger than Houston. It signals the ambition.

speaker: NORA
text: And then Levine Leichtman.

speaker: JAMES
text: In February 2024, Levine Leichtman announced it had acquired USA Water from Warren Equity, in partnership with management. The terms weren't disclosed. The advisers were Kirkland and Ellis for Levine Leichtman, and Harris Williams and Holland and Knight for USA Water. The trade headline at the time was, more or less, USA Water switches sponsors.

speaker: NORA
text: So in six years it's had two private equity owners.

speaker: JAMES
text: Two, in a fairly short span. That's not unusual for a buy-and-build platform. The first owner assembles it and proves the model. The second owner, usually with a bigger fund, takes it further, more acquisitions, more geography. Levine Leichtman's stated plan was growth through acquisitions and expansion into new geographies.

speaker: NORA
text: Were there other investors along the way?

speaker: JAMES
text: One aggregator, PitchBook, lists other investors including CNL Strategic Capital and Churchill Asset Management, and shows about ninety-one million dollars raised across seven rounds. I'd be cautious with that. Aggregator figures for private companies are estimates, and they can mix equity and debt in ways that aren't obvious.

speaker: NORA
text: And acquisitions since Levine Leichtman came in?

speaker: JAMES
text: This is where the record gets thin. PitchBook lists five add-on acquisitions since 2024. Eom Public Works in June 2024. AWR Services in August 2024. Florida Utility Solutions in May 2025. And Tindall Enterprises and Southeastern Environmental Services, both in August 2025. We couldn't confirm any of these against a company press release. And other sources disagree: Warren Equity's page mentions four add-ons without naming them, and one trade article said two. So the honest summary is a handful of add-ons, likely including a push into Florida and the Southeast, but unverified.

speaker: NORA
text: And news this year?

speaker: JAMES
text: None that we found. No 2026 announcements from the company or about its leadership. Which, for a business like this, isn't necessarily a bad sign. Contract operators often grow quietly. But it does mean we're reading the strategy from the outside.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about who actually hires USA Water. You keep saying utility districts. What are those?
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: JAMES
text: This is a bit of general background, and I'll keep it careful. In Texas, and especially around Houston, a lot of suburban growth has been financed through special districts. A developer builds a new subdivision, and a local district is created to build and run the water, sewer and drainage infrastructure, funded by bonds and paid back through local taxes and fees. Those districts are often run by small elected boards of residents.
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: NORA
text: So a board of five neighbours is suddenly responsible for a water plant.
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: JAMES
text: More or less. And they don't have staff. They're not going to hire their own licensed operators, lab technicians, maintenance crews and billing clerks. So they hire professionals. Typically a lawyer, an engineer, a bookkeeper, and an operator. The operator is the company that actually runs the system day to day. That's the role Si Environmental built its business on.
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: NORA
text: And outside Texas?
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: JAMES
text: The same logic applies to small and mid-sized municipalities across the country. Industry research from Bluefield, which tracks this market, lists the reasons utilities outsource: aging infrastructure, regulatory demands, financial constraints, workforce shortages and rising costs. If you're a small town and your one licensed operator retires, you have a real problem. A contract operator can step in tomorrow.
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: NORA
text: What does the customer actually care about? If I'm on one of these boards, what makes me happy?
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, four things, in roughly this order. First, no violations. A boil-water notice or a sewage overflow is a nightmare for a small board. Second, reliability: the water's on, the pumps work, problems are fixed quickly. Third, cost predictability, because the board answers to residents who pay the bills. And fourth, communication. Board members want a clear monthly report that tells them what happened and what's coming.
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: NORA
text: Not innovation, then.
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: JAMES
text: Not as a headline, no. Nobody on a district board wakes up wanting AI. They want fewer surprises. If AI shows up for them, it will show up as fewer violations, faster fixes, better reports and steadier costs. That's an important framing for everything we'll say about technology today.
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: NORA
text: And how sticky are these customers?
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find data on churn or contract length, so this is our inference. Contract operations is the kind of service that's hard to switch. A new operator has to learn the system, the quirks of each plant, the history of each problem. Boards tend not to change operators over small price differences, because the risk of a bad transition is high. That's a strength. But it also means when you do lose a client, it's usually because something went wrong on service.
chapter: The customer: districts and small towns

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go inside the work. What does running a water system involve?

speaker: JAMES
text: On the drinking water side, you're producing water, usually from wells or a surface source, treating it, typically disinfecting it, storing it in tanks and pushing it through the network at the right pressure. Operators check chemical levels, take samples for testing, keep records, and respond to alarms. On the wastewater side, you're collecting sewage through pipes and lift stations, treating it at a plant, and discharging clean effluent under a permit with limits.

speaker: NORA
text: And all of that is regulated.

speaker: JAMES
text: Heavily. Federal law sets the framework, the Safe Drinking Water Act for drinking water and the Clean Water Act for discharges, and states run most of the day-to-day oversight. In Texas, that's the state environmental regulator. Operators generally need state licences at different grades depending on the system. And there's a constant stream of sampling, monitoring and reporting obligations. Miss a sample or a report, and you can have a violation even if the water was fine.

speaker: NORA
text: So paperwork is part of the product.

speaker: JAMES
text: Paperwork is a big part of the product. Levine Leichtman's description of USA Water explicitly includes regulatory compliance as a core service. When a board hires an operator, they're buying the confidence that every required sample was taken, every report was filed and every record could survive an inspection.

speaker: NORA
text: What about maintenance?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the other big chunk. Pumps, motors, valves, blowers at the wastewater plant, chemical feed systems, generators, meters. Things wear out. Some maintenance is scheduled, some is emergency. A lift station pump fails at two in the morning, and someone has to go out before the wet well overflows. Emergency work is expensive, overtime-heavy and stressful. Reducing it is one of the clearest ways to improve a contract's economics.

speaker: NORA
text: And billing?

speaker: JAMES
text: Si Environmental already provided customer billing at the time of the 2020 deal, and today there's a vice president for billing and technical services. For a utility district, that means reading meters, producing bills, collecting payments and handling customer calls. It's a high-volume, rules-heavy back-office service, and that matters for AI, because back-office text and numbers are where today's AI tools are strongest.

speaker: NORA
text: What technology does an operator like this typically use?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, the systems often have SCADA, which stands for supervisory control and data acquisition. It's the industrial control and monitoring layer: sensors, alarms, remote readings of levels, flows and pressures. Some have geographic information systems mapping their pipes, and asset management software. But here's a caution. We did not find any public evidence of which systems USA Water uses or how its data is organised. And in a business built by acquisition, serving many separate clients, it's very likely the technology varies a lot from site to site.

speaker: NORA
text: And the client owns the SCADA, not the operator.

speaker: JAMES
text: Often, yes. Which matters for data rights. If USA Water wants to build predictive models on SCADA data, it has to work within whatever its clients allow.

speaker: NORA
text: One more on the work itself. How is an operator business actually staffed?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general terms, and this is industry background rather than anything USA Water has published, you have licensed operators running routes, often with a mix of licence grades because bigger or more complex plants need more senior people. Behind them sit maintenance technicians, electricians and mechanics who handle repairs. Then supervisors who plan the work, a compliance function that tracks every sampling and reporting deadline, and back-office teams for billing and accounts. And there's an on-call rota, because water systems don't keep office hours.

speaker: NORA
text: So the cost base is basically people and vehicles.

speaker: JAMES
text: People, vehicles, parts, chemicals in some contracts, and lab fees. Mostly people. Which is why everything we'll say about AI comes back to how many systems each skilled person can look after safely.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make this concrete. Give me a hypothetical day. An invented operator, not a real person.

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's call him Marcus. He's a licensed operator for a contract firm like USA Water, and he covers a route of, say, six utility districts in the suburbs west of a big city. Each district has a small water plant, a wastewater plant or a connection to a regional one, and a few lift stations.

speaker: NORA
text: What does his morning look like?

speaker: JAMES
text: He starts at the first water plant around six. He checks the chlorine residual, looks at the tank levels, listens to the pumps, glances at the chemical feed. He writes the readings on a log sheet or enters them in a tablet. Then he drives to the next site and does it again. By mid-morning he's taken the samples due today, which go to a lab. One lift station had a high-level alarm overnight, so he checks the floats and the pump run times and finds one pump is drawing more current than it should.

speaker: NORA
text: So that's a maintenance ticket.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. He calls or messages the maintenance supervisor, who schedules a crew. If that pump fails completely before the crew gets there, it becomes a night call-out. Meanwhile, a resident calls the district's billing line complaining about a high bill, and the billing team needs to know whether a meter was misread or there's a leak.

speaker: NORA
text: And the afternoon?

speaker: JAMES
text: More rounds, plus paperwork. Monthly operating reports for the state. A summary for the district board meeting next week. Someone has to pull together the readings, the work orders, the sample results, any exceptions, and turn them into a report the board can understand. In many operations, that's still done by hand from logs, spreadsheets and emails.

speaker: NORA
text: So where's the waste in Marcus's day?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, three places. Driving and routine checking at sites where nothing has changed. Re-typing readings and assembling reports. And the reactive call-out that could have been a planned repair if someone had spotted the trend in that pump a week earlier. None of those are Marcus's fault. They're the shape of the work.

speaker: NORA
text: And the thing he's actually expert at?

speaker: JAMES
text: Judgement. Knowing that this plant always smells a bit odd after heavy rain but that one doesn't. Knowing which board member wants a phone call before anything goes in the report. That knowledge lives in Marcus's head, and in a workforce that's getting older, that's a real risk for the business.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's widen out. How big is this market?

speaker: JAMES
text: The best figure we found comes from Bluefield Research, which describes third-party operations and maintenance for US drinking water and wastewater utilities as valued at nearly three billion dollars a year. Their page is dated late 2024, and it doesn't say which year the valuation refers to. So treat it as an order of magnitude: a market in the low billions, not the tens of billions.

speaker: NORA
text: And growth?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find a reliable growth rate, so I won't give one. What we can say is that the drivers Bluefield lists, aging infrastructure, regulation, money pressure and workforce shortages, are all long-term and all point toward more outsourcing, not less. That's our view, not a forecast.

speaker: NORA
text: Who are the competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: There's a mix. At the large end there's Veolia North America, part of the big French environmental services group, which runs contract operations among many other things. Jacobs, the large engineering firm, has an operations and maintenance business. Inframark operates municipal water and wastewater systems. Woodard and Curran is an engineering and operations firm. Alliance Water Resources is another operations peer. And then there's U.S. Water Services Corporation, an employee-owned firm based in Florida.

speaker: NORA
text: Tell me about that one, since it sounds like the closest match.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's the closest scale peer we found. Founded in 2003, employee-owned, and in 2022 it bought the operations and maintenance business of the engineering firm Ramboll in the Americas. After that deal it described itself as about seven hundred professionals across eighteen states. That gives you a sense of what a scaled contract operator looks like. And it's a Florida firm, which matters if USA Water is pushing into Florida too.

speaker: NORA
text: And American Water?

speaker: JAMES
text: American Water is a different model, but it competes for the same small systems. It's a large regulated utility, and rather than operating systems under contract, it buys them outright. In June 2026, it announced it had completed a purchase of Nexus Water Group systems in eight states, for about three hundred and fifteen million dollars. When a big utility buys a small system, that system no longer needs a contract operator.

speaker: NORA
text: So for USA Water, a district selling itself to American Water is a lost customer.

speaker: JAMES
text: Potentially, yes. That's the consolidation threat. A small system has a few choices. Run it yourself, hire an operator, or sell to a big utility. As the big utilities get more active, the pool of systems that want an operator could shrink in some places.

speaker: NORA
text: What's USA Water's edge against the big names?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, local density and relationships. In contract operations, being close matters. If you have dozens of districts in one metro area, your operators' routes are short, your maintenance crews can reach a failure fast, and you can share specialists. A national giant might have scale overall but less density in a specific suburb. And Si Environmental's leadership says its team has two hundred and thirty-eight years of combined experience, by its own count. That's a company that knows its districts.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the acquisition strategy, because I think it's central to the investment.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. The contract operations market is fragmented. There are many small and regional operators, often founder-owned, often run by people who came up as operators themselves. A platform like USA Water can buy those firms, keep their client relationships and local crews, and give them better back-office support, procurement, safety programmes and technology.

speaker: NORA
text: What does each acquisition actually give them?

speaker: JAMES
text: Contracts, mostly. Each add-on brings a portfolio of districts or municipalities, the operators who know them, and sometimes a new geography. If the PitchBook list is right, Florida Utility Solutions and Southeastern Environmental Services sound like moves into Florida and the Southeast, though we couldn't confirm what those businesses do.

speaker: NORA
text: And what's hard about it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integration, as always. Every small operator has its own way of logging rounds, its own spreadsheets, its own billing software, its own maintenance tracking, if it has any. Its own culture. When you buy five of them in eighteen months, you inherit five ways of doing everything. The benefit of the platform only shows up when you bring some of that together.

speaker: NORA
text: Bring together what, specifically?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd prioritise three things. A common way of recording operator rounds and readings. A common maintenance and work-order system. And a common billing platform where the company does billing. Those are the systems that touch every contract, every day. They're also, not by coincidence, the foundations any AI would need.

speaker: NORA
text: So integration and AI are really the same project.

speaker: JAMES
text: In a business like this, I think so. You can't run AI on data that lives in twelve different spreadsheets formatted twelve different ways. The first AI job at a buy-and-build platform is usually joining up data across the acquired businesses. That's not glamorous, but it's where the value starts.

speaker: NORA
text: What about pricing on acquisitions?

speaker: JAMES
text: There's a subtler lever. When a platform buys a small operator, it often finds contracts priced below market, or without proper cost escalation, because the founder never wanted to rock the boat with the board. Over time, the platform can bring those contracts to a fair price at renewal, tied to its costs. Done badly, that annoys clients. Done well, with better service and better reporting to justify it, it's a meaningful source of margin. That's our view of how these platforms typically work.

speaker: NORA
text: So, the AI question. Where is USA Water today?
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: Honestly, we found no company-specific evidence of AI at all. The 2024 announcement from Levine Leichtman talks about acquisitions and geographic expansion, not technology platforms or AI. The trade coverage didn't mention technology. The leadership page lists no AI or data roles. And as we said, we couldn't review the holding company's own site.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: No evidence isn't the same as nothing happening.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: That's right, and I want to be fair. Plenty of companies in this sector use software every day without talking about it. They may well have digital logging, work-order systems or remote monitoring at some sites. We just can't see it. What we can say is that AI isn't part of how the company presents itself publicly.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: Is that unusual for the water sector?
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: Not really. Water utilities are conservative, for good reasons. You don't experiment with the system that keeps people from getting sick. That said, there's movement. There's an American Society of Civil Engineers journal paper surveying AI adoption in US drinking water operations, which tells you the profession is studying it seriously. We only saw the title, not the findings, so I won't characterise them. And the trade press has started using the phrase augmented operator, the idea that AI's role is to help a shrinking pool of licensed operators do more, not to replace them.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: I like that framing.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: So do I, and I think it fits USA Water well. The company's product is skilled people. The scarce resource in the industry is skilled people. AI that makes each operator more effective attacks the constraint directly.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: What about the cybersecurity side? I know that's been in the news.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: It has. In July 2026, there were reports of a sweeping cyberattack on water systems in multiple US states, and federal officials were reported to be on edge about it. Separately, a Senate committee advanced the 2026 Water Resources Development Act, which is the regular federal water infrastructure bill, with provisions expanding cybersecurity support for water systems. We only saw headlines on both, so I'll keep it at that. But the direction is clear. Water systems are a target, and anyone operating them, including contract operators, is under pressure to take cyber seriously.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: And how does that interact with AI?
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: JAMES
text: It cuts both ways. Connecting more systems and pulling more data into the cloud to run models can increase the attack surface if it's done carelessly. But AI is also used for spotting unusual activity on networks. For a contract operator, I'd say the order matters: get the security basics right first, then add the clever stuff.
chapter: Where USA Water is with AI

speaker: NORA
text: Let's name the challenges. What's hard for USA Water, in your view?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name five. First, the workforce. The whole industry is short of licensed operators, and USA Water's growth depends on hiring, training and keeping them. Every new contract needs people. Every retirement takes knowledge out of the business.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Integration load. Two sponsor changes in about four years, plus a series of add-ons, means a lot of change for a mid-sized company. The leadership team has to run the existing contracts, absorb acquisitions and, presumably, prepare for the next owner one day. That's a lot of plates spinning.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fragmented systems and data, which we've talked about. Many clients, many plants, many different control systems owned by different districts, and acquired businesses with their own tools. It's hard to get one clear picture.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth.

speaker: JAMES
text: Regional concentration. Texas and the Southeast are good places to be, with population growth and lots of new districts. But concentration means exposure to regional risks, including the weather. Hurricanes, floods and freezes all hit water systems hard, and a contract operator is the one on the front line when they do.

speaker: NORA
text: Say more about that. Why does weather matter so much?

speaker: JAMES
text: As general background, Texas has had some severe reminders. The winter storm in February 2021 caused widespread power and water problems across the state, with many systems issuing boil-water notices. The Gulf Coast also gets hurricanes and flooding. When power fails, lift stations stop unless generators kick in. When pipes freeze, they burst. When floods hit, treatment plants can be overwhelmed.

speaker: NORA
text: And the operator gets the call.

speaker: JAMES
text: The operator gets every call. That's where a contract operator earns its reputation, or loses it. Having enough crews, generators, spare pumps and a clear emergency plan across dozens of districts at once is a real operational capability. In my view, it's also a place where better data helps: knowing which lift stations have backup power, which tanks are low, which sites flood first. That's not fancy AI, it's good situational awareness, and it's the foundation for anything more sophisticated later.

speaker: NORA
text: And fifth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Visibility, which is partly our problem as researchers but also, I'd argue, a business issue. The public picture of USA Water is inconsistent. Two headquarters, an outdated chief executive listing on one aggregator, conflicting add-on counts. That doesn't affect a district board, which knows its operator personally. But when you want to recruit operators, win municipal contracts outside your home market, or one day tell your story to a buyer, a clear and consistent public presence helps. In my view, that inconsistency is also a small hint that data hygiene inside the business may be uneven, though that's an inference.

speaker: NORA
text: And the AI-specific challenge?

speaker: JAMES
text: The revenue model. Contract operations are usually priced around the labour and costs needed to run the system. If AI genuinely cuts operator hours per contract, clients will eventually ask why the fee hasn't come down. So USA Water has to think about whether savings go to margin, to the client, or into better service. That's a commercial question as much as a technical one.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's move to opportunities. If you were advising USA Water, where would you look first?

speaker: JAMES
text: The first and biggest is automating operator rounds and compliance reporting. Every contract involves recurring rounds, readings, samples and reports. That's the largest recurring labour cost in the business, and the work repeats across every district. A digital round with an AI assistant could log readings by voice or photo, flag anything out of range against that site's history, and draft the monthly operating report and the board summary automatically for a human to check.

speaker: NORA
text: What's the value?

speaker: JAMES
text: Labour hours per contract, plus fewer compliance slips. We didn't find any public figure for either at USA Water, so I won't invent one. But if an operator spends a meaningful part of each week on paperwork, giving even a slice of that back means more districts per operator. In a labour-constrained market, that's growth capacity, not just cost saving.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Predictive maintenance on the clients' SCADA and asset data. Pump current, run times, vibration where it's measured, flows and levels. A model can spot that a pump is drifting from its normal pattern days before it fails. That turns a two a.m. emergency into a planned Tuesday repair. The lever is margin on each contract through less overtime and fewer emergency parts orders. And it's a better story for the board: fewer overflows, fewer outages.

speaker: NORA
text: But you said the data may not be there.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the catch. We couldn't confirm what SCADA, mapping or asset management systems are in use across USA Water's clients. So predictive maintenance is probably a second-wave project, after the data foundations are in place. I'd start it at the few sites with the best instrumentation and prove it there.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Billing and customer service. USA Water bills customers for at least some districts. AI is well suited to billing exceptions: flagging a reading that looks wrong, spotting a probable leak from a usage spike, drafting a clear explanation for the resident, and handling routine calls like payment dates or service starts. Lower handling cost, fewer billing errors, happier residents and happier boards.

speaker: NORA
text: What else?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, pricing and contract discipline. Tie renewals to cost indices and use service data to show the board what they're getting. If you can show a district that you hit every sample, responded to every alarm within a set time and cut emergency call-outs, you have a strong case for a fair price. Fifth, continued acquisitions into new geographies, which is the stated plan. And sixth, industrial operations and maintenance as an adjacency. The U.S. Water Services deal with Ramboll shows there's a sizeable industrial market next door, though we have no evidence USA Water is pursuing it.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a knowledge opportunity, given what you said about Marcus?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, and I'd add it to the list. Capturing operator know-how. Site notes, past problems, the fix that worked last time, all searchable by the next operator on that route. An assistant that can answer, what happened the last time this lift station alarmed after heavy rain? That protects the business against retirements and speeds up training new operators.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go back to the pricing worry for a moment, because I think it's the trickiest part. If AI makes the work cheaper, how should USA Water charge for it?

speaker: JAMES
text: There are a few models, and this is our view rather than anything the company has said. One is to keep the fee and raise the service level: same price, but faster response times, better reporting, fewer violations. Another is to share a defined slice of savings with the client, which builds trust. A third is to move part of the fee toward outcomes, for example a bonus for zero compliance violations or for keeping unplanned outages under a threshold.

speaker: NORA
text: Would a small district board actually want an outcome-based contract?

speaker: JAMES
text: Some would, some wouldn't. Boards like predictability, so a big variable component could worry them. I'd start with a small performance element on top of a stable base fee. The real point is that the operator needs to measure outcomes well before it can price on them. Which, again, comes back to clean, consistent data from every site.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI bet for the next eighteen months, what is it?

speaker: JAMES
text: Operator rounds and compliance reporting. It's the biggest recurring cost, it repeats across every contract, the risk is manageable because a licensed human still reviews and signs off, and it doesn't depend on getting access to every client's control system. You can start with a tablet and a well-designed form.

speaker: NORA
text: Give me the first hundred days.

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: pick one region, ideally a cluster of districts around Houston where the operating practices are most mature. Map exactly how rounds are logged today, what reports are produced for whom, and how long each takes. Agree three measures: operator hours on paperwork per district, report errors or late filings, and operator satisfaction, because if the operators hate it, it won't stick.

speaker: NORA
text: Days thirty to sixty?

speaker: JAMES
text: Roll out a simple digital round on tablets in that cluster, if it isn't already there, with consistent fields across every site. Then add an assistant that drafts the monthly operating report and the board summary from those readings and the work orders. Run it in parallel: the operator or supervisor still produces their usual report, and you compare the two.

speaker: NORA
text: Shadow mode again.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's essential in a regulated service. You never want an AI-drafted report going to a regulator that nobody checked. Days sixty to a hundred: switch the pilot cluster to the AI-drafted reports with human review and sign-off, measure the time saved and the error rate, and decide on rollout to the next region, including the acquired businesses. At day one hundred, you should have real numbers instead of a hypothesis.

speaker: NORA
text: Who owns it?

speaker: JAMES
text: One named leader with operations credibility, not just technology credibility. The operators need to see that it was built by people who understand the work. I'd pair that person with whoever owns billing and technical services today, because that team already sits at the junction of operations and systems.

speaker: NORA
text: And what about the governance side?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three rules from the start. A licensed human signs every compliance submission. Client data stays within the terms each district has agreed. And anything that touches control systems gets a security review before it goes anywhere near production. Write those down, share them with clients, and you've turned a risk into a selling point.

speaker: NORA
text: And the second-best bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Predictive maintenance at the best-instrumented sites. It has a bigger potential payoff per site, but it needs better data, so it comes second.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do one more hypothetical, from the customer's side this time. An invented district, invented board.
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: JAMES
text: Picture a district of a few thousand homes on the edge of a growing metro. The board meets monthly in the evening. Five residents, a lawyer, the district engineer, and the operator's account manager, who we'll call Dana.
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: NORA
text: What happens today?
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: JAMES
text: Dana brings a printed operations report. Water pumped, wastewater treated, sample results, any violations, work orders completed, repairs recommended, billing figures, delinquent accounts. Somebody in her office spent most of a day assembling it from logs and spreadsheets. The board flips through it. One member asks why the electricity bill at the wastewater plant jumped. Dana doesn't have the answer with her and promises to follow up.
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: NORA
text: And with the tools you described?
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: JAMES
text: The report is drafted automatically from the digital rounds, the work-order system and the billing platform, and Dana reviews and edits it in an hour instead of a day. It includes a short plain-English summary at the top: what went well, what needs a decision, what's coming. And it flags in advance that the blower at the wastewater plant ran longer than normal, which explains the electricity jump, with a recommendation to inspect the diffusers.
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: NORA
text: So the board gets the answer before it asks the question.
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the goal. And notice what that does commercially. The board sees a professional, proactive operator. When the contract comes up for renewal, Dana's company isn't competing on price alone. It's competing on visible competence. That's why I keep saying AI for a company like this is as much about the client relationship as it is about cost.
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: NORA
text: What about the residents?
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: JAMES
text: If the billing assistant spots a usage spike at a home that suggests a leak, it can trigger a friendly notice before the resident gets a shocking bill. That's fewer angry phone calls, fewer disputes at board meetings, and fewer write-offs. Small things, but they add up across thousands of accounts.
chapter: A second walk-through: the board meeting

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other businesses, especially services companies owned by private equity, learn from USA Water?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four lessons. First, in a services business, AI is a capacity tool before it's a cost tool. When your growth is limited by how many skilled people you can hire, giving each person back a few hours a week is effectively hiring. Frame it that way internally and your people will see it as help, not as a threat.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, integration is the AI strategy in a buy-and-build. Before you can do anything clever, you need the same data recorded the same way across every acquired business. The platform that standardises its rounds, work orders and billing first will be the one that can actually use AI later.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, think about your pricing before your customers do. If AI makes your work cheaper to deliver, a smart client will eventually notice. Decide in advance how you'll share the value: maybe better service levels at the same price, maybe outcome-based fees tied to compliance and reliability. Don't wait to be asked.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, tell your story. In a quiet industry, a company that clearly explains how it uses technology to deliver safer, more reliable service will stand out, to clients, to recruits and, eventually, to buyers. Right now USA Water's public story is thin and inconsistent. That's easy to fix and, in my view, worth fixing.

speaker: NORA
text: I'd add one from what you said about Marcus. Capture the knowledge before it walks out the door.

speaker: JAMES
text: Agreed. Any business with an ageing skilled workforce should be asking, where does our expertise actually live, and what happens when those people retire? AI-searchable site notes are one of the cheapest insurance policies you can buy.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, consolidation by larger players. American Water's Nexus purchase shows big utilities buying small systems, which can take potential clients out of the operator market and push prices. Two, AI reshaping the revenue model. If AI cuts hours and clients push to share the savings, fee-based contracts could shrink unless USA Water moves toward pricing on outcomes. That's our inference, but it follows from the logic.

speaker: NORA
text: Three?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three, AI-enabled challengers. A software-first operator, with heavy automation and remote monitoring, could bid lower on labour-heavy contracts. We haven't seen that happen at scale in this market, but it's a plausible threat. Four, municipal in-sourcing. Some cities may bring work back in-house if they can hire operators, though the labour shortage makes that hard. And five, cyber and regulatory risk. A breach or a serious compliance failure at a client could cost contracts and create liability.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there an AI-specific risk inside the operation itself?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. If an assistant drafts compliance reports, it could get something wrong, a misread value, a missing sample, a sentence that sounds right and isn't. In a regulated service, that's serious. The defence is design: the AI drafts from structured readings rather than inventing text, every number traces back to a logged reading, and a licensed person reviews and signs. Over-reliance is the quieter risk. If operators stop looking closely because the system usually gets it right, mistakes slip through. Training and spot audits matter.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owners?

speaker: JAMES
text: Execution on the buy-and-build. Levine Leichtman bought the business in early 2024, so we're nearly three years into the hold. The value story at exit will rest on how many contracts it has, how well it integrated them, and whether it has a credible operating platform. AI that has demonstrably increased operator capacity would strengthen that story a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three things. First, confirmation of the add-ons, ideally a press release that names the acquired businesses and the new regions. Second, any announcement of a common operating platform, digital rounds, work-order systems or remote monitoring across the group. And third, any public statement on cybersecurity, given the attacks on water systems this year. If USA Water publishes something on how it protects client systems, that's a sign of maturity.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: What does USA Water sell?

speaker: JAMES
text: Licensed people, maintenance and compliance for other people's water systems.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Its operators and their relationships with dozens of local utility districts.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: Very little public visibility, and probably fragmented systems from acquisitions.

speaker: NORA
text: Shipped AI feature?

speaker: JAMES
text: None that we could find.

speaker: NORA
text: Best AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Digital operator rounds with AI-drafted compliance and board reports.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI replace water operators?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. It will help fewer operators run more systems, which the industry badly needs.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a district board member should ask their operator this year?

speaker: JAMES
text: How do you protect our control systems from a cyberattack, and can you show me?

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Optimist on the business, which is steady and needed. Cautious on technology until we see evidence.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. USA Water was formed in 2020 by Warren Equity Partners around Si Environmental, a Houston-area contract operator founded in 2012 that served more than eighty utility districts. In February 2024, Levine Leichtman bought it, with chief executive Jeff Haley staying on and a plan built on acquisitions and new geographies, with several add-ons reported since, although we couldn't confirm them. The company runs water and wastewater systems for districts and municipalities that can't easily staff them, in a market one research firm puts at nearly three billion dollars a year, driven by aging infrastructure, regulation and a shortage of operators. We found no public evidence of AI at USA Water. The best opportunity, in our view, is digital operator rounds with AI-drafted compliance reports, followed by predictive maintenance where the data allows. The challenges are the workforce, integrating acquired businesses, and making sure AI savings don't simply turn into lower fees.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the bigger lesson is that in an essential service built on scarce skilled people, the best use of AI isn't replacing anyone. It's letting every operator look after more of the systems we all depend on, more safely.

speaker: NORA
text: Next time on Portfolio Deep Dives, episode eighteen, we head to Cleveland and NSL Analytical, a materials testing lab where accreditations are everything and the report is the product.

speaker: JAMES
text: See you then.
